verses.text: After that, Paul left Athens and went to Corinth.

There he met a Jewish man named Aquila, originally from Pontus. Aquila had recently arrived from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Emperor Claudius had ordered all Jews to leave Rome. Paul went to see them,
and because they shared the same trade, he stayed and worked with them. They made tents for a living.
Every Sabbath Paul reasoned in the synagogue, trying to persuade both Jews and Greeks.
When Silas and Timothy came down from Macedonia, Paul devoted himself to preaching. He testified to the Jews that Jesus is the Messiah.
But when they opposed him and insulted the message, he shook the dust from his clothes and said, “You’re responsible for what happens now! I’ve done my part. From here on, I’m going to the Gentiles.”
He left and went to the home of a man named Titius Justus, who worshiped God. His house was right next door to the synagogue.
Crispus, the synagogue leader, believed in the Lord, along with everyone in his household. Many Corinthians who heard Paul believed and were baptized.
One night the Lord told Paul in a vision, “Don’t be afraid. Keep speaking; don’t go silent.
“I’m with you. No one will attack or hurt you, because I have many people in this city.”
Paul stayed there for a year and six months, teaching God’s message among them.
But when Gallio became governor of Achaia, the Jews united against Paul and brought him before the court.
They accused him, “This man is persuading people to worship God in ways that break the law.”
Paul was about to answer, but Gallio said to the Jews, “If this were about a crime or serious wrongdoing, I’d have reason to hear you out.
“But if this is about words, names, and your own law, handle it yourselves. I’m not going to judge these matters.”
Then he drove them away from the court.
The crowd grabbed Sosthenes, the synagogue leader, and beat him right there in front of the court. Gallio didn’t care at all.
Paul stayed on in Corinth for many more days. Then he said goodbye to the believers and sailed for Syria with Priscilla and Aquila. In Cenchreae he had his hair cut because of a vow.
They arrived in Ephesus, where Paul left Priscilla and Aquila. He went into the synagogue and reasoned with the Jews.
They asked him to stay longer, but he declined.
As he left, he said, “I’ll come back to you if God wills. I have to get to Jerusalem for the coming festival.” Then he sailed from Ephesus.
After landing in Caesarea, he went up to greet the church, then traveled down to Antioch.
He spent some time there, then traveled through Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples along the way.
Meanwhile, a Jewish man named Apollos arrived in Ephesus from Alexandria. He was an eloquent speaker and knew the Scriptures well.
He had been taught the Lord’s way and spoke about Jesus with great passion and accuracy, though he knew only John’s baptism.
Apollos began speaking boldly in the synagogue. When Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained God’s way to him more accurately.

Apollos wanted to cross over to Achaia, so the believers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples there, asking them to welcome him. When he arrived, he greatly helped those who had believed through grace,
because he powerfully showed from the Scriptures, in public debate, that Jesus is the Messiah.
